source.title: Acute Kinematic and Kinetic Adaptations to Wearable Resistance During Sprint Acceleration

paper.citation: Macadam P, Simperingham KD, Cronin JB. Acute kinematic and kinetic adaptations to wearable resistance during sprint acceleration. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(5):1297-1304.
paper.abstract: This acute study examined how wearable resistance of 3% body mass (BM), attached to the anterior or posterior lower limbs, changed sprint acceleration mechanics in 19 male rugby athletes. Each athlete completed 20 m maximal sprints unloaded and with each placement, in one session. Step, split, velocity, force-velocity and vertical stiffness measures were compared with unloaded sprints.
paper.tldr: In one session, 3% BM on the anterior or posterior lower limbs slowed the 10 to 20 m split and lowered estimated theoretical maximum velocity (V0), with no difference between placements. The study did not test whether the load improves sprint performance, so coaches who use it should track their athletes' own sprint times.
paper.methods: Nineteen male rugby athletes completed six 20 m sprints, two per condition, in randomized order with 4 minutes of passive rest between trials. Loads were attached in compression shorts and calf sleeves, with two-thirds of the load on the thigh and one-third on the shank. Steps and contact times were measured with Optojump, horizontal velocity with a Stalker ATS II radar, and V0, F0 and Pmax were modelled from the velocity data, with conditions compared by repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: The 10 to 20 m split was significantly slower with the load (1.35 s unloaded, 1.38 s anterior and 1.39 s posterior), and estimated V0 was significantly lower (8.32 m/s unloaded, 7.87 m/s anterior and 7.78 m/s posterior), while 0 to 10 m and 20 m times did not change significantly. Contact time was significantly longer in both the start and acceleration phases, acceleration-phase step frequency was lower, and the F-v slope changed by -10.9% anterior and -10.5% posterior, which the authors describe as a more force-dominant profile. F0 and Pmax did not change significantly, and anterior and posterior placements did not differ significantly on any variable.
paper.limitations: The study is acute, descriptive and based on one session with a single 3% BM load, with no joint-angle measurement and no training period, so it does not test the abstract's claim that the load may enhance sprint acceleration performance. The sample was male rugby athletes aged 18 to 22 years with at least two years of sprint training, and several mean differences were smaller than the SDs, so individual athletes may respond differently. A co-author received funding from the company that supplies the garments, and several percentages in the text do not match the printed means (for example, start-phase vertical stiffness, acceleration-phase posterior stiffness and F0), so the source PDF should be checked before quoting them.
paper.practicalImplications: If a coach uses a load like this, keep it to early-acceleration work rather than max-velocity running, since the split and V0 changes were the clearest effects. Track each athlete's own sprint times with the load, because group means may not match an individual's response. The rise in contact time and the shift in the F-v profile may matter if the aim is to change force production, but this paper did not test whether that improves sprint performance.
paper.athleteDev: In male rugby athletes, 3% BM wearable resistance slowed the 10 to 20 m split and lowered estimated V0 while changing contact time and step frequency. The study does not establish a sprint performance benefit, so it should not be used to claim that the load improves speed.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested acute sprints in male rugby athletes in one session and measured no return-to-play outcome, and the paper does not print injury screening criteria, so its loaded-sprint changes should not be used to judge readiness after injury.
